answer.line: The lens forms from surface ectoderm, after the optic vesicle grows out from the brain and touches it.

steps: Trace the induction. The optic vesicle grows out of the forebrain and touches the surface ectoderm of the head.
That touch tells the surface ectoderm to thicken into a lens placode, fold in and pinch off as the lens.
So the retina comes from the brain side, and the lens from the outer layer the brain reached out and touched.

choices.note: Neural crest builds the cornea's middle layer and the iris stroma, which makes it tempting. The lens comes from the surface layer instead.
Both build parts of the eye: muscles, vessels, corneal layers. Neither one makes the lens.
Surface ectoderm, induced by the optic vesicle.
Head mesoderm makes the muscles that move the eye and its blood vessels, not the clear lens.
Endoderm lines the gut tube and the organs that bud from it. It never reaches the surface of the head.

lockIt: The lens is surface ectoderm, induced by the optic vesicle; the retina comes from the brain.

visual.alt: A fate map from the three germ layers. Ectoderm, outlined as the answer, splits into surface ectoderm, neural tube and neural crest; the lens sits under surface ectoderm, and a green path runs from it back up to ectoderm. Mesoderm builds the eye muscles and vessels, and endoderm the gut lining.
visual.caption: Follow the green path up from the lens. It never passes through the crest, mesoderm or endoderm.
